4.21.s.en: The bride shares with her Bridegroom

4.21.0.en: "Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind, blow upon my garden, that its spices may flow out.

4.21.1.en: Let my beloved come down to His garden, and eat His precious fruit" [16].

4.21.2.en: At the wedding feast the Bridegroom praised His bride and called her to go out with Him outside the camp, to share His sufferings and His crucifixion, and to be anointed with myrrh and so be buried with Him, that she might rise with Him bearing many and varied plants, which are the work of His resurrection in her. Now the bride addresses Him and asks that the north wind, full of cold, and the hot south wind blow upon her garden... so that her spices may flow out, and her Bridegroom may come down to her and enjoy His fruits in her... What, then, does the bride mean by the north wind and the south wind? 1. In Greek the word "wind" is the same as the word "spirit"... Perhaps the bride here is asking her Bridegroom to send her His Holy Spirit, who pursues her from every side, so that He may give her the abundant fruit in which the Bridegroom rejoices. 2. The call to the wind to blow upon her is a call to the Beloved Himself, as the gentle and meek wind who passes through the heart and dwells in it, so that "the work of Christ" may be done in us. 3. Perhaps the soul meant by the wind some outward circumstances, for since she has become a closed garden consecrated to the Lord, she is not afraid of what surrounds her, for "all things work together for good to them that love God" (Rom 8:28). If the Apostle Paul was given honor, it turned out to the furtherance of the Gospel, and if he was bound in the inner prison, his bonds turned out all the more to the furtherance of the Gospel (Phil 1:12), or as he says of himself, "Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death" (Phil 1:20). 4. The wind also signifies trials, for if northern trials blow upon the soul, that is, if sin is stirred up against her, or right-hand trials, as when self-righteousness rises up within her... in all this the Lord upholds her, not only to keep her from trials but to bring forth from them fruits in which the Bridegroom rejoices! He is like Samson, who brought forth food out of the eater, and found sweetness in the strong!

4.21.3.en: It is to be noted that the soul calls her heart "my garden," that is, her own, but she quickly calls her Bridegroom, saying, "Let my beloved come down to His garden." For she is His vineyard, the work of His hands and under His care; He is in the midst of her, so she shall not be moved. The soul cannot let her spices flow in the midst of trials unless she surrenders herself to Him to be His garden, that He may care for her and eat of her fruit, which is "His fruit."

4.21.4.en: She calls Him to come down to her, for the heart is His, and the fruit is ascribed to Him... St. Ambrose saw that the call is directed to the Bridegroom to come down to the soul in the font of Baptism, to receive His garden and work in it by His Holy Spirit so that she may bring forth His fruit, as he says:

4.21.5.en: ["Let my beloved come down to His garden, and eat the fruit of the apple tree that is His." Truly, what a beautiful tree, full of fruit, whose roots stretch out in the waters (of Baptism) of the holy spring!]. He came down to her by His Incarnation, by His crucifixion and His entering the tomb, and He comes down to her at her baptism in the holy spring, and she still asks Him to come down to her, coming upon the clouds, to take her with Him, for she has borne His fruits within her!

5.1.0.en: No sooner had the Church called her Bridegroom to come down to her to eat from His garden within her, full of the plants of His Holy Spirit and watered from the holy spring of Baptism, than He answered her call at once without hesitation, saying:

5.1.1.en: "I have come down into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb (my bread) with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk; eat, O friends; drink, and be drunk, O beloved" [1].

5.1.2.en: He hastened to come down to His garden without hesitation, because the call here accorded with His will, and so found a swift response in the eyes of God. She called Him to come down to His garden, to which He desires to come down at all times. For if the Lord from eternity prepared the events of salvation so that they became the object of His delight and pleasure, in spite of the shame, suffering, and death they carried, as the Apostle Paul says: "for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb 12:3), then His bride calls Him to come down to the very garden He entered on the night of His passion, and to that in which His body was laid in the tomb. She calls Him to see her as she fills up what is lacking of the afflictions in her body (Col 1:24), that is, shares His sufferings and His crucifixion and His burial; therefore the Lord does not hesitate to say: "I have gathered my myrrh with my spices"... as though the events of salvation had become alive and extended in the life of His children!

5.1.3.en: Father Rufinus sees that the garden here is none other than the place where the Lord was crucified, where the wise man declares that the Bridegroom drinks wine mingled with myrrh, which was offered to the Lord at the moment of His crucifixion.

5.1.4.en: The Lord accepted the call at once, for He found that everything that belongs to the bride is His own: her title is His garden, and she is His sister and His bride, and within her He found His myrrh and His spices, His honeycomb and His honey, His wine and His milk. He found the fruits of His Holy Spirit within her and hastened to her, and He found within her no hire of iniquity or hire of a harlot or any other of the things that He does not accept, as He says: "Thou shalt not bring the hire of a whore, or the price of a dog, into the house of the LORD thy God for any vow: for even both these are abomination unto the LORD thy God" (Deut 23:18).

5.1.5.en: Before explaining what is inside the garden, St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, asked:

5.1.6.en: "Who is this whom she invites to the banquet that she has prepared?"

5.1.7.en: He is the One from whom and by whom all things exist (1 Cor 1:17), who gives help to everyone in due season (Lk 12:43), who opens His hand and satisfies every living thing with blessing (Ps 145:16), who comes down as the heavenly Bread (Jn 6:14), giving life to the world, and pours out from Himself alone life upon all creation.

5.1.8.en: This is the One for whom the bride prepared her table, and the table is a garden planted with living trees. The trees are we ourselves, and the fruit that we offer is our souls, as He said when He took on the fullness of our humanity: "My meat is to do the will of my Father" (Jn 4:34). The aim of His divine will is plain, for He wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4).

5.1.9.en: Therefore the food that is prepared is our salvation, and the fruit is our free will, which offers to God "our souls," as though they were fruit gathered from the branch.

5.1.10.en: It is fitting for us also to contemplate the bride, who formerly enjoyed the fruit of the apple tree, saying: "his fruit was sweet to my taste" (Song 2:3); but now she herself has become sweet, a ripe fruit offered to the vinedresser, who enjoys it.

5.1.11.en: As for the expression "Let my beloved come down" [1], it is in its wording a petition like the prayers "Hallowed be thy name" and "Thy will be done." Just as the form of these two phrases carries a prayer, so the bride prays, saying: "Let (my friend) come down," declaring to God the abundance of the fruit of her perfection.

5.1.12.en: His coming down requires the work of His divine love, for we cannot ascend to the Most High unless the Lord stands by the lowly and lifts up the meek (Ps 147:6) [Ps 146 LXX].

5.1.13.en: So that the soul may rise to heaven, she seeks the help of God on high, beseeching Him to come down from His majesty and be united with us here who are below.

5.1.14.en: The answer came through the prophet thus: "Then shalt thou call... and he shall say, Here I am" (Isa 58:9); indeed, even before the bride lifts up her prayer He hears her petition and gives ear to the preparation of her heart [(Ps 10:17) Septuagint].

5.1.15.en: He comes to His garden... and gathers its spices, full of the fruit of her virtues; then He speaks of His enjoyment of the banquet and His delight in it, saying to His bride: "I have come down into my garden, my sister, my bride...".

5.1.16.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa He comes down into the heart and dwells in it and rests; He gathers its myrrh with its spices... that is, He gathers the fruits of the Cross (the myrrh) with the blessings of His holy tomb (the spices). He sees that the cup of our myrrh is His own cup, and the spices with which we are shrouded are the spices of His burial... He sees us bearing His cross and buried with Him to the world.

5.1.17.en: Within us He eats His honeycomb and His honey, as though He had entered the Promised Land that flows with milk and honey. He eats the same two kinds of food, "the honeycomb and the honey," of which He ate with His disciples after His resurrection, proving in many ways that He is alive, risen from the dead, remaining at work in the midst of His Church.

5.1.18.en: He finds everything in our heart sweet and delectable, like the honeycomb and the honey.

5.1.19.en: He drinks also His wine, that is, His love which He poured into us by His Holy Spirit, with His unadulterated milk, that is, purity and chastity...

5.1.20.en: Then He invites His friends and His beloved to enter with Him into His own garden, that they may be satisfied and rejoice over His bride. Who are these friends and beloved? They are the heavenly ones who rejoice over one sinner who repents more than over ninety and nine just persons who need no repentance (Lk 15:7). These enter the heart with the Lord not to reign but as soldiers of the heavenly King, friends of the Bridegroom, saying with St. John the Baptist: "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice" (Jn 3:29).

5.1.21.en: The following are excerpts from the sayings of the Fathers about these friends and their work in the heart:

5.1.22.en: * The heart is the palace of Christ; into it the King enters to rest, and with Him the angels and the spirits of the saints; there He dwells and walks, and within it He establishes His kingdom!

5.1.23.en: St. Macarius the Great * He does not stand alone, but the angels go before Him, saying: "Lift up your gates, O ye princes." Which gates are these? Those of which the psalmist sings in another place, saying: "Open to me the gates of righteousness" (Ps 19:1).

5.1.24.en: Therefore open your gates to Christ, that He may enter into you; open the gates of purity, the gates of courage, the gates of wisdom.

5.1.25.en: Believe the message of the angels: Lift up your everlasting gates, that the King of glory may come in, the Lord of Sabaoth (of hosts).

5.1.26.en: St. Ambrose Therefore let us open the heart to God and His angels, that there may be heavenly joy within us.

5.2.0.en: "I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved (my near one) that knocketh, saying,

5.2.1.en: Open, open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.

5.2.2.en: I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on?

5.2.3.en: I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?" [2-3].

5.2.4.en: What an accurate picture of the mutual dealings between God and man! For a long time man lived relaxed and neglectful of his salvation, in spite of all the means God gave him to be watchful. God wanted to make him a son of light and of the day, but man insisted on turning all the time of his exile into night, which he spends asleep, even though his heart is awake.

5.2.5.en: God gave humanity the natural law to awaken their hearts, so that they are without excuse; but "when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things" (Rom 1:21-23).

5.2.6.en: And He gave them the written Law, but since they sinned in the Law, they fell under judgment by the Law, "for not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified" (Rom 2:13); so the holy Law, or the commandment which is holy, and just, and good, revealed sin to me and exposed it, so sin revived and I died (Rom 7).

5.2.7.en: And God sent His prophets, but what did humanity do to them? The Lord Himself says: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37).

5.2.8.en: And finally, "the voice of my beloved that knocketh"... The Word of God Himself came down to man to knock at the door of his heart... He stands before the soul begging her to open to Him. The Sun of Righteousness came down and entered our time, which we had made night, to shine upon us who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, that we might arise from our heedlessness!

5.2.9.en: Perhaps the discourse here concerns the soul that called the Messiah her Bridegroom, but then relaxed in her love for Him. Sleep overcame her and she could not watch with Him on the night of His passion, though her heart, the dwelling of the Holy Spirit, in which there is life, rebukes her! She grew lukewarm in her love for Him, but God, the Lover of mankind, sees her heart awake and does not cease to come down to her door and call her: "Open, open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my perfect one..."

5.2.10.en: The voice of the Beloved here reproaches gently, so that it does not wound the feelings of the heart, but encourages His bride, calling her His sister, His friend, His dove, His perfect one... though she is sound asleep! He does not rebuke her nor reprove her, but gives her hope and encourages her.

5.2.11.en: As for His repeating the request: "Open, open to me..." it may perhaps show the repeated call to humanity in the two Testaments, the Old and the New, for God has not changed, nor has His call changed, since He asks that the heart open to Him and receive Him!

5.2.12.en: In the repetition of the call there is also a declaration of the perfect freedom of the soul, for He is the Creator and Lord and King, yet He does not force His way into the soul, but entreats her to open to Him... In the book of Revelation we see Him say: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me" (Rev 3:20); even when He came to His disciples walking on the sea in the midst of the great tempest, He did not force His way into their boat, but the Evangelist says: "Then they willingly received him into the ship" (Jn 6:20).

5.2.13.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic used this friendly speech of the Lord Christ to the human soul in his book "History of the Arians" as an argument against their use of violence, saying: [When He (the Lord) comes to anyone He does not need to open by force, but He knocks at the door, saying: "Open to me, my sister, my bride"; if it is opened to Him, He enters, and if it delays, He departs and does not enter. He uses persuasion and counsel when He preaches the truth, and does not use swords and soldiers. But what persuasion is this, when the terror of the emperor prevails?!].

5.2.14.en: He persuades her to open to Him by love, for she has become His sister and He her firstborn brother, who is able to help her. He became "the firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:39); He broke through the door of death and shattered it, becoming the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Cor 15:20)... Let her open her heart to Him who opened for her the door of life!

5.2.15.en: He returns and begs her to open by the strong friendship between them, for He calls her "His friend," which is the title by which Abraham, the father of believers, was called (2 Chr 20:7; Isa 41:8; Jas 2:23). If God opened the secrets of His heart to His friend Abraham, saying: "Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do?" (Gen 18:17)... how much more fitting it is for the believer, who has become a friend of God, to open his heart fully to Him.

5.2.16.en: He draws her to open the doors of her heart by calling her "His dove," since she bore within her the "Holy Spirit," who came down in the form of a dove, and so she has the power to open her heart.

5.2.17.en: And finally He encourages her to do so, since she is "the perfect one" who is without blemish, so she cannot close the door in His face.

5.2.18.en: Thus God deals with us: He instructs us not through commands and prohibitions but by declaring His love and friendship, and makes clear to us our standing in relation to Him, and reveals to us the potentialities of His Holy Spirit working in us, and encourages us by what we have attained!

5.2.19.en: Finally He entreats her as the "bearer of sorrows and griefs" for her sake, saying to her:

5.2.20.en: "For my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night" [2].

5.2.21.en: If you have made your time a night without day, so that your life has become sleep, then in love I break into time and enter this night, not to sleep but to bear the terrors of the night for you. Indeed the Lord entered the garden at night while His disciples slept and could not watch with Him one hour (Mt 26:40), but He went into the depths to receive the cup of suffering that He might drink it for all humanity... In the garden He "began to be sorrowful and very heavy" (Mt 26:37). He cried: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death," and the drops of sweat poured down like blood!!!

5.2.22.en: He speaks to her and asks her to open to Him for the sake of what He endured on her account that stormy, rainy night, for His head was filled with dew and His locks with the drops of the night... He bore the divine wrath in His body, and as the prophet says: "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:4-5).

5.2.23.en: But she offered unfitting human excuses and spoke without concern; she did not call Him her Lord or her master, nor even call Him by His name, nor mention any of His titles, but said:

5.2.24.en: "I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on?!

5.3.0.en: I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?" [3].

5.3.1.en: What feeble arguments the soul presents in her spiritual lukewarmness... an excuse for not opening the heart to the One of whom she knows fully that He loves her. It is a picture of man, who begrudged himself bearing a little weariness to achieve the meeting with the Lord Christ, in spite of the great deal that the Lord paid!

5.3.2.en: How easy it would be for her to wrap a garment around her body and put sandals on her feet... but she was preoccupied with the comfort of her body rather than the enjoyment of her Bridegroom... she resembled those who made excuses so as not to attend the wedding (Mt 22:5).

5.3.3.en: If she has put off her coat, the Lord Christ Himself is the eternal garment that covers us, as the Apostle Paul says: "ye have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27).

5.3.4.en: This is the best robe which the heavenly Father brings to the son who returns to Him (Lk 15:22). This is the embroidered garment offered by the hand of God, as the prophet Zechariah says: "I have taken away thine iniquity from thee, and clothed thee with embroidered garments" (Zech 3:4).

5.3.5.en: If she has put off her garment, He gives her His Spirit to put on, as the secret of life within her, for He assures His disciples: "Behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high" (Lk 24:49).

5.3.6.en: If she has washed her feet, let her know that the One knocking at the door is her Lord, who girds Himself and washes the feet of His bride (Jn 13:5). She washed them with the water of her own righteousness so that her conscience might rest for a while, but when the hands of the Lord reach out to wash her feet she will have rest in His eternal kingdom. Therefore the Lord said to the Apostle Peter: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" (Jn 13:8). Therefore let us rise from the bed of the "ego," or the "human self," and go to our Bridegroom, who covers us with His blood and clothes us with His Holy Spirit, and also washes our inner life so that we may live as holy to Him.

5.4.s.en: Married love returns through the Cross

5.4.0.en: If the soul cannot listen to the voice of the One who loved her, who declared His love in various ways, there remains for Him to stretch out His wounded hand on the Cross into her mind, that she may see the marks of the wounds of love which He bore for her sake, and her bowels groan for Him, as she says:

5.4.1.en: "My beloved put forth His hand through the window, and my bowels groaned for Him; I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with flowing myrrh upon the handle of the lock" [4-5].

5.4.2.en: When the world grew narrow before the disciples because of fear, they shut the doors and set up barricades, not knowing that closed doors would not prevent the Lord, wounded for their sake, from entering to them to show them His hands and His side so that they rejoiced (Jn 20:20). He opened an inner window in their hearts so that they might touch the wounds of His love. Thus the Lord puts forth His wounded hand through the window so that His believers may discover the secret of His love and their bowels groan for Him. I say that this window is none other than the side of the Lord and His wounds, through which the Lord puts forth the hand of His love so that we uncover His inner bowels aflame with love, and our bowels also groan... He loved us first, therefore we also love Him.

5.4.3.en: The window has special memories in the Old Testament, some of which carried symbolic aspects of God's saving work in the life of His bride; we mention by way of example: 1. Through the window Abimelech perceived that Rebekah was Isaac's wife and not merely his sister (Gen 26:8), and likewise through the wounds of the Lord the Church is declared the bride of Christ Jesus. 2. Through the window the two spies were let down from Rahab's house, which was on the town wall (Josh 2:15), and through it David descended from the house, fleeing from Saul's messengers, and escaped (1 Sam 19:21). Through the window we descend from the pride of this world to cross its walls and escape all the counsels of the devil. 3. The window on which she bound a cord of scarlet threads (Josh 2:12), and through which Rahab the harlot and all her household were saved, is a reference to the wounds of the Lord Christ, which rescued the corrupt company of the Gentiles and all their children who entered the Church, kept in the precious blood of the Lord. 4. As the window was a sign of salvation, it also bore a sign of the destruction of evil, for when Jezebel the wicked queen painted her eyes and adorned her head with the adornment of the world, she was thrown down from the window and the dogs licked her blood (2 Kgs 9). And Ahaziah the wicked king too, who trusted in Baalzebub the god of Ekron and not in the living God, fell down through the lattice in his upper chamber that was in Samaria (2 Kgs 1:2), and was sick and died. And in the song of Deborah the judge, she asked the mother of King Sisera to look out of the window (Judg 5:28) to see why the chariots of her son were so long in coming and why the steps of his chariots tarried... for he and his chariots perished. 5. Through this window the bowels of believers groan for the saving love of God, while unbelievers mock these wounds, imitating Michal the daughter of the wicked king Saul, for when she looked through a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord she despised him in her heart (2 Sam 6:16; 1 Chr 15:29).

5.4.4.en: We return to the bride, who enjoyed the hand of the Lord that came into her midst and so perceived the secret of His Cross; the hardness of her stony heart was broken, and she arose to open to her beloved. She cried out with the younger son: "I will arise and go to my father" (Lk 15). She declared her longing for the One who loved her by returning to Him through sincere repentance, bitter tears, and pure sighs; therefore she said: "my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with flowing myrrh upon the handle of the lock."

5.5.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the myrrh signifies "the death which Christ died for us," for we have touched it through repentance and accepted to die with Him, so that the everlasting doors may be opened before us.

5.5.1.en: "I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had turned and passed on.

5.5.2.en: My soul went out when He turned away (spoke).

5.5.3.en: I sought Him, but I did not find Him; I called Him, but He gave me no answer.

5.5.4.en: The watchmen that go about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me.

5.5.5.en: The keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.

5.5.6.en: I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem (by the powers of the field and its virtues), if ye find my beloved, that ye tell Him that I am wounded with love.

5.5.7.en: What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women!!

5.5.8.en: What is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us!" [6-9].

5.5.9.en: She arose to open to her Bridegroom after a long sleep, but her Bridegroom had left her and passed on. Why did He do so? He disciplines man for his delay in responding, and in His discipline He appears as though He had left us for a time... This leaving in itself is considered a sign of God's concern for us, and Father Daniel gave two reasons for this leaving: 1. God leaves us for a short time that we may be alerted to the weakness of our hearts; then we realize that whatever purity of heart we had before was a free gift through divine visitation. 2. When He leaves us, our heart's aim and our zeal in prayer in seeking the Holy Spirit are revealed within us, that is, it serves as a test for us in perseverance, steadfastness of mind, and true zeal. So when we obtain spiritual happiness and the joy of purity, we hold on to these things with more care, because men in general do not care to keep what they think they can obtain easily.

5.5.10.en: Father Daniel says: [The blessed prophet David makes known to us that this temporary forsaking on God's part is sometimes for our good, and therefore he asked in his prayer that this forsaking not be perpetual, beseeching Him that it be within certain limits, saying: "O forsake me not utterly" (Ps 119:8). In other words he says: I know that You forsake Your saints for their benefit and in order to test them... Therefore I do not ask that You not forsake me, for it is not profitable for me not to feel my weakness (therefore he said: "and it seems to me that I have been humbled" (Ps 119:71)), nor is it of benefit to me not to have an opportunity for battle. For this opportunity will surely not be given me as long as I am filled with God's constant protection. For Satan does not dare to fight me as long as I rely upon Your protection... So I ask You to leave me, but not utterly (the Greek expression "not exceedingly"), for it is useful for me that You leave me a little so that the steadfastness of my love may be tested...].

5.5.11.en: Father Daniel spoke much about what we call spiritual lukewarmness because of God's leaving us for a time so that we may be tested, fight, and be proved... but in truth it is not forsaking but divine care, and St. John Chrysostom likened God's attitude to a nurse who holds a child's hands, walks with him a little, then suddenly lifts her hands from him so that he may dare to walk... She takes away her hands but continues to look at him with her heart and mind as her eyes watch him, and her hands are ready to support him.

5.5.12.en: The human soul says: "I sought Him, but I did not find Him," though He stands beside her, indeed He is within her, waiting to see her striving for His sake, so that she may say with Jacob: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."

5.5.13.en: "I called Him, but He gave me no answer," though He is occupied with arranging all things for my salvation.

5.5.14.en: The soul went about the whole world seeking the One she loves though He was within her, and as St. Augustine said: [In his folly he went out to search for Him outside, in nature and in books, though God was within him, deeper than his depth and higher than his height].

5.5.15.en: Now who are the watchmen that go about the city who smote her and wounded her, and the keepers of the walls who took away her veil from her? 1. Since the speaker here is the believer in the Church of the New Testament, he reproaches in the name of the Church the company of the Jews and their leaders, who represent the watchmen going about the city of Jerusalem and those responsible for guarding the word of God, since it was fitting for them to be servants of the Word and preachers of the Messiah the Savior, but they seize the Church and smite her and wound her, and have come to defame her...

5.5.16.en: Before these insults the believer does not turn his gaze away from his Bridegroom, but on the contrary assures those who trouble him that he is wounded by the love of this heavenly Bridegroom, saying: "I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem... if ye find my beloved, that ye tell Him that I am wounded with love."

5.5.17.en: This is the fifth time that the Church of the Gentiles speaks with the company of the Jews in reproach thus:

5.5.18.en: a. In the first instance (Song 1:5), she reproaches them because they insulted her, saying of her that she is black like the tents of Kedar, has no origin, did not receive the Law, and no prophets came from her... She answers them that though she is black by virtue of her pagan origin, yet now she is in the bosom of the Father, who joined her to Himself and made her comely through His Son Jesus Christ, who made her comely and made her like the curtains of Solomon.

5.5.19.en: b. In the second instance (Song 2:7), when she began her union with the Lord, whose left hand is under her head and whose right hand embraces her, the Jews tried to corrupt and destroy this union; but she declared that the day comes in which the Lord will appear and declare the truth of this union.

5.5.20.en: c. And in the third instance (Song 3:5), when the Bridegroom entered the tomb the Jews stood in the position of those who gloat, as though saying: "Come out of the tomb and we will believe you"; but the Church answers them: Do not suppose that He died and His message passed away, but He is alive, risen from the dead, raising me up with Him and bringing me up from the wilderness white as pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense... through Him she rose to the Father!

5.5.21.en: d. And in the fourth instance (Song 3:11), when the discourse was about the Cross, the Church asked the Jews to understand that when they crowned Him with thorns in mockery, He was in fact being crowned as the Bridegroom of all humanity on the day of His wedding and the day of the gladness of His heart.

5.5.22.en: e. This is the fifth time (Song 5:8), where the Church declares to the company of the Jews that though her children passed through some lukewarmness, and it became as though God had forsaken them, yet the Church is still alive, full of love... She strives until the Lord removes their lukewarmness from them. 2. Perhaps the watchmen going about the city refer to the servants of the Church, the city of God, and the keepers of the walls are the preachers of the word; all of these are bound to hide behind the word of God in their speaking with lukewarm souls. These souls feel as though they were smitten by them and wounded, and put to shame and disgrace by the taking away of their veil, because the word of God is like a sword that cuts off evil and drives it away from the soul. It is also like a mirror that exposes man's weaknesses and unveils his depths! So the blows and wounds and nakedness here are not meant to trouble the soul and defame her, but are the wounds of love that lead to sincere repentance. As the Apostle Paul himself says: "For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me?" (2 Cor 2:2).

5.5.23.en: In any case, when lukewarmness is removed from the human soul, she not only realizes her return to the Father's embrace in Christ Jesus, but she bears witness to the power of this work even before unbelievers, who ask, saying:

5.5.24.en: "What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women!

5.6.0.en: What is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?!" [9].

5.6.1.en: You are beautiful and lack nothing, so who is this Beloved with whom you are occupied? Who is this unique Beloved by whom you thus charge us for the sake of your remaining in union with Him?!

5.6.2.en: Perhaps in this question there is a prophecy of the Jews' acceptance of the Lord Christ in the last days, for there comes a day in which the Jews will realize that they err in seeking an earthly kingdom and temporal ambitions, whereas the need is for eternal salvation and a tasting of God's heavenly love!

5.7.0.en: 1. The bride praises her Bridegroom. 2. The dialogue of the garden. 3. A description of the bride "Shulamite."

5.8.0.en: When the world discovers in the bride her love for her Bridegroom and realizes the effectiveness of this love in her inner life and its reflections on her features, her feelings, and her conduct, it asks about this unique Bridegroom. Here the bride bears witness to her Bridegroom not by words but by the life she lives, for she knows Him fully and touches Him, being united with Him; He brings her into the knowledge of the invisible Father... She bears true and practical witness, saying of Him: 1. "My beloved (my friend) is white and ruddy" [10].

5.8.1.en: How sweet is this Savior-Bridegroom, for in Him the two colors, white and red, are joined, each making the other clear and complete! He is white, but not the pale white that is lifeless, like Ananias the high priest, of whom the Apostle Paul said: "God shall smite thee, thou whited wall: for sittest thou to judge me after the law, and commandest me to be smitten contrary to the law?" (Acts 23:3); for by his violation of the commandment and the Law he came under the sentence of death without life, for he lost his blood, the sign of life, and became pale like the dead; but the Savior of the Church in His whiteness bears a constant redness, a sign of perfection of strength, life, and vitality! Likewise the Savior does not bear redness apart from whiteness, otherwise there would be in that an indication of killing and bloodshed, as in the book of Revelation (Rev 6:4), and as sin is described as scarlet and red like crimson (Isa 1:18); but He is "he that cometh from Edom, with red garments from Bozrah, this that is glorious in his apparel... I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save" (Isa 63:1).

5.8.2.en: The word "white" here came in the sense of "radiant," for He is the Sun of Righteousness who shone upon us who sit in darkness, to bring us by His Holy Spirit into the fullness of the light of the knowledge of the Father. We were carried in Him through His radiance in the merits of His blood (the red), to be in the bosom of the Father and know the fullness of His mysteries. Thus His radiance is mingled with His saving work, that is, His whiteness with His redness, so that we may bear the reflections of His radiance in us by our entering to His Father.

5.8.3.en: In the book of Daniel we see His clothing white as snow (Dan 7:2), and at His Transfiguration also "his raiment was white as the light" (Mt 17:2). And what is the garment of the Lord Christ but His Church, in which He wraps Himself like a garment, dwelling within her? So the radiance and whiteness He bears He reflects on His Church, as on the heavenly ones who are in His presence always (Mk 16:5; Acts 1:10), so that we appear in heaven in white garments (Rev 3:4; 7:9), as we are enjoined thus: "Let thy garments be always white" (Eccl 9:8).

5.8.4.en: Holy Scripture speaks of many appearances of angels but does not go into describing their garments; yet in the events of the Resurrection and the Ascension Scripture assures us that the angels appeared in white garments. They appeared for our sake, that we may know that through the Lord's resurrection and ascension we are washed and made whiter than snow (Ps 50). If our sins were like scarlet - they were buried in the tomb - the Lord raised us up like snow (Isa 1:18); therefore the prophet Daniel says: "Ye shall be purified and made white" (Dan 11:35).

5.8.5.en: Thus the Church sees her Bridegroom and rejoices in His radiance and is glad in His blood... but the enemy Satan trembles before the radiance of the Savior and fears the blood of His Cross; therefore the Church says: 2. "A banner among ten thousand" [10].

5.8.6.en: He became known to men and demons: the Church knows Him as "standing for an ensign of the people" (Isa 11:10); He was lifted up on the Cross and drew humanity to Himself, to pour His radiance on it and sanctify it with blood; and the demons know Him and cry out: "Come down from the cross," because He destroyed their kingdom and made a public show of them, triumphing over them (Col 2:15).

5.9.0.en: 3. "His head is fine gold (pure), His locks are flowing, black as a raven" [11].

5.9.1.en: If gold signifies heavenly life, then "pure gold" signifies His divinity, for in Him "dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (Col 2:9). The Father appointed Him head of the Church, "from which all the body by joints and bands" (Col 2:9), for He alone, as the Son of God and His Word, is able to bring the whole body into heaven. If the head is heavenly, the body cannot live except on a heavenly level as long as the body is united with the head. This is the secret of her love for her Bridegroom, that He brings her into the heavens, that is, into the bosom of His Father, through her union with Him.

5.9.2.en: As for His flowing hair that surrounds the Church, it is the Church, or as St. Augustine says: [It is the company of the saints, who are like the hair of the Lord; not one of them falls without the permission of His Father... they live by Him. Therefore no white hair appears in Him, but He is entirely "black as a raven"; no believer grows old, but renews his youth like the eagle].

5.9.3.en: This is the work of the Holy Spirit, who grants fellowship between the members and the Head, so the members remain in the fullness of their strength through the Head, who never weakens at all.

5.9.4.en: Just as the Lord Christ is "the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 12:8), so His Church passes through Him beyond the bounds of time, so that old age does not touch her, nor do earthly events prevail against her!

5.10.0.en: 4. "His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk, sitting in their sockets (by the streams)" [12].

5.10.1.en: Though He is the awesome King who frightens the enemies, with eyes like a flame of fire (Rev 1:14), searching the details of things and their hidden parts, yet when He appears to His believers they see His eyes like the simple, gentle dove, full of innocence. His eyes are like the eyes of the dove, "of purer eyes than to behold evil" (Hab 1:13).

5.10.2.en: Father Victorinus, bishop of Pateu, a man of the third century, sees that the waters signify the many diverse peoples who came to God through Baptism; thus the speech about His eyes being like doves by the rivers of waters signifies the Lord's Incarnation and the declaration of the beginning of a new holy generation through His baptism.

5.10.3.en: As for their being washed in milk, this signifies the Lord's concern to offer His believers pure, unadulterated faith as nourishment for their souls, for St. Ambrose says: [The Lord is baptized in milk, that is, He is baptized in sincerity, and those baptized in milk are those who have the faith without defilement].

5.10.4.en: As for their sitting in their sockets, that is, their resting in their place, it signifies God's care for His Church and His children; He fixes His divine gaze on every member, and does not turn His eyes from him until He brings him into the fellowship of the glories.

5.10.5.en: We can also say that the eyes of Christ are His priests and servants, those who bear the look of Christ toward humanity, who have spiritual insight opened by the Holy Spirit as "by the Dove," to bring peoples into the waters of Baptism, where they are washed of their sins and enjoy unadulterated faith like milk. These workers sit in their sockets, that is, they have a place in the Head, "Christ," so that through Him they can look upon every soul, concerned for the salvation of all. Their likening to the eyes of Christ is scriptural, for in the Old Testament the prophet was known as the seer (Amos 7:12), since the prophet by the spirit of prophecy can see what the people cannot see. He was sometimes called the watchman (Ezek 3:17; 23:7), who stands on the tower to see whether there are enemies and warns the people.

5.11.0.en: 5. "His cheeks are like a thicket (bowl) of spice, and beds (overflowing) of fragrant herbs" [13].

5.11.1.en: The cheeks of the Lord Christ, which refer to His countenance, were exposed to mockery and contempt, as Isaiah the prophet says: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and disgrace" (Isa 50:6)... This face, which the Lord did not turn away from the spitting of the wicked (Mt 27:3), the Church sees bearing signs of self-giving love, so it is likened to a thicket of spice, that is, a group of interwoven shrubs that diffuse a sweet fragrance, and to beds (bouquets) of fragrant herbs, which the soul smells as a fragrance of life. 6. "His lips are lilies, dropping flowing myrrh" [13].

5.11.2.en: We spoke before about the Bridegroom as the lily of the wilderness, and that by union with Him believers also become lilies. But here the lips of the Bridegroom are likened to lilies (the lily flower)... What does this mean?

5.11.3.en: The lily signifies royal glory, for the Lord speaks of it, saying: "even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these" (Mt 6:29). So the lips of the Lord Christ proclaim glorious teachings, or in other words offer the word of life that is able to bring the believer into the glorious eternal life. Therefore the psalmist says of Him: "grace is poured upon His lips" (Ps 45:2).

5.11.4.en: These lips bear a fragrant perfume that drops like myrrh. The Evangelists described the words that came from them thus: "Never man spake like this man" (Jn 7:47), "And all bare him witness, and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth. And they said, Is not this Joseph's son?" (Lk 4:22).

5.11.5.en: As for describing them as dropping myrrh mingled with liquid myrrh, it means that His words are mingled with entering into the bitterness of His sufferings and being buried with Him, since He was shrouded with liquid myrrh... Everyone who hears Him longs to enter with Him into the fellowship of His sufferings and to die with Him. As St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [Myrrh pours forth from His body and fills the souls of those who received Him, and this is a clear symbol of the mortification of the body...].

5.11.6.en: St. Gregory also sees that this mouth overflowing with lilies and flowing myrrh represents the Apostles, who are the mouth of the Lord, witnessing by the word of His Gospel, which is the lily, and bringing believers into the flowing myrrh, that is, fidelity in Baptism, or burial with Him, that they may receive the power of His resurrection. The Apostle Peter poured out a radiant lily, which is the Word, in the house of Cornelius, filling the souls of his hearers with myrrh, for they were buried with the Lord Christ in Baptism and became dead to the world.
